seo_desc: Degenerative disc disease treatment in North Palm Beach. One-on-one physical therapy to build strength, ease flare-ups and keep you active. Medicare accepted.
lede: Physical therapy for degenerative disc disease that builds a stronger, more resilient back so flare-ups bother you less and everyday activity feels manageable again.
what_it_is: The discs between your vertebrae are rubbery cushions that let your spine bend and absorb load. With age they dry out, lose height and can develop small tears or cracks. Despite its name, Cleveland Clinic describes degenerative disc disease as a condition that occurs when spinal discs wear down. When the changes irritate nearby tissues or nerves, they can cause back pain or pain that spreads into a leg.

Disc wear is close to universal. Cleveland Clinic reports that almost everyone has some disc degeneration after age 40, yet it leads to back pain in only about 5% of adults. A 2015 systematic review in the American Journal of Neuroradiology found disc degeneration on imaging in 37% of 20-year-olds and 96% of 80-year-olds who had no back pain at all. Cleveland Clinic lists physically demanding work, smoking, obesity and injuries such as falls as risk factors.
symptoms: Low back pain that comes and goes, with flare-ups lasting weeks or months
Pain that worsens with sitting, bending or lifting
A sharp, aching or stiff feeling in the lower back
Pain that spreads into the buttocks or legs
Tingling or numbness in a leg
Leg weakness in more severe cases
causes: Natural aging and loss of water in the discs
Physically demanding work or frequent heavy lifting
A sudden injury such as a fall

how_therapy_helps.intro: Because disc changes show up in so many people without pain, therapy focuses on how your back moves and tolerates load. The 2021 JOSPT low back pain guideline gives its strongest grade to exercise for chronic low back pain, including strengthening, endurance, aerobic and general exercise. It also gives a strong recommendation to joint mobilization and to pain neuroscience education delivered alongside exercise or manual therapy. Cleveland Clinic lists physical therapy among the main nonsurgical treatments.
methods: A progressive program for the trunk, hips and legs helps your spine tolerate sitting, bending and lifting, the activities that most often set off disc pain.
Walking or cycling at a comfortable pace builds fitness without jarring the spine. The JOSPT guideline supports aerobic and general exercise for chronic low back pain.
Learning that disc wear is a normal part of aging, and how pain and sensitivity work, helps reduce fear of movement. The guideline recommends pairing this education with exercise.
Skilled hands-on techniques can ease stiffness and pain in the lower back, making it easier to stay active between flare-ups.
You practice controlled bending and lifting and learn how to scale activity during a flare rather than stopping altogether.

first_visit: Expect your first visit to last about an hour. Your therapist asks about your flare-up pattern and which activities, such as sitting, bending or lifting, set it off. Bring any imaging reports you have. The exam looks at lower back and hip movement, trunk and leg strength and endurance, and how you control bending and lifting. If pain travels into a leg, sensation, reflexes and muscle strength are checked too. You start treatment and a home program that day.
recovery: Degenerative disc disease is best thought of as something you manage over time. Cleveland Clinic describes pain that comes and goes, with episodes lasting weeks or months, and notes that ongoing exercise is needed to keep symptoms under control. There is no fixed recovery timeline, and progress depends on how long you have had symptoms, your fitness and the demands of your work. Many people find flare-ups become less frequent or easier to handle as strength and confidence improve.
self_care: Use heat, ice or gentle stretching to ease a flare
Keep up low-impact activity such as walking during a flare, at a lower dose
Stand up and move every so often during long stretches of sitting
Lift with your legs and keep loads close to your body
see_a_doctor: Any loss of bladder or bowel control, which needs emergency care
Leg weakness or difficulty walking that is getting worse
Numbness in the groin or inner thighs
Back pain that began with a hard fall or a car accident
Severe pain that does not ease with rest or position changes

faqs.q: Is degenerative disc disease really a disease?
faqs.a: Not in the usual sense. Cleveland Clinic explains that degenerative disc disease is a condition that occurs when spinal discs wear down, and it says almost everyone has some disc degeneration after age 40. The label describes age-related changes that sometimes cause pain. Many people with the same changes on a scan have no symptoms at all.

faqs.q: Does degenerative disc disease always cause pain?
faqs.a: No. Cleveland Clinic reports that disc degeneration leads to back pain in only about 5% of adults. A 2015 systematic review in the American Journal of Neuroradiology found degeneration on imaging in 68% of 40-year-olds and 80% of 50-year-olds who had no back pain. Its authors concluded that many of these changes may be part of normal aging.

faqs.q: Can physical therapy reverse degenerative disc disease?
faqs.a: Physical therapy is not designed to change how a disc looks on an X-ray or MRI. Its goal is to reduce pain and improve what you can do. The 2021 JOSPT low back pain guideline strongly supports exercise for chronic low back pain, and stronger, better-conditioned muscles can help your spine handle daily loads with fewer flare-ups.

faqs.q: What is the best exercise for degenerative disc disease?
faqs.a: No single exercise works for everyone. The 2021 JOSPT low back pain guideline supports several types for chronic back pain, including trunk strengthening, endurance training, aerobic exercise, aquatic exercise and general exercise. Cleveland Clinic suggests low-impact options such as walking. The best choice is one you can do regularly without a lasting increase in pain.

faqs.q: Will degenerative disc disease lead to surgery?
faqs.a: Most people manage without it. Cleveland Clinic lists physical therapy, anti-inflammatory medication, injections and self-care such as low-impact exercise and stretching as nonsurgical options, and notes that surgery is considered when those approaches fail and pain persists. A physician makes that decision with you, usually after a period of conservative care.

faqs.q: Can degenerative disc disease cause leg pain?
faqs.a: It can. Johns Hopkins Medicine notes that disc and joint wear in the lower back can cause pain in the back and buttocks that sometimes spreads into the thighs, which may mean a nerve is involved. Cleveland Clinic explains that worn discs can tear and irritate or press on nearby nerves. Leg weakness, numbness that keeps worsening, or any change in bladder or bowel control needs prompt medical attention.

notes_for_reviewer: ICD-10 M51.36 (Other intervertebral disc degeneration, lumbar region) is now a non-billable parent (verified on icd10data.com). Billable children: M51.360 with discogenic back pain only, M51.361 with lower extremity pain only, M51.362 with both, M51.369 without mention of either.
Page is written with a lumbar focus to fit the back-pain hub; cervical DDD is not covered.

JOSPT 2021 CPG grades used: exercise for chronic LBP (Grade A), thrust or nonthrust joint mobilization for chronic LBP (Grade A), pain neuroscience education alongside other interventions (Grade A), movement control or trunk mobility exercise (Grade B). The CPG addresses chronic LBP generally, not DDD specifically.
Cleveland Clinic states 'women are more likely to experience symptoms'; omitted from risk factors to keep claims conservative.
Sources are adequate but DDD-specific treatment evidence is thin; recommendations rely on the general chronic LBP guideline. Only 4 sources.
